lines.text: You will hear a man talking to a community group about a new bike-share scheme in their city. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Evening, everyone, and thanks for coming along. My name's Rob Hennessy, and I'm the project coordinator for CityCycle, the new bike-share scheme that's launching here in Westbury next month. I'll explain how it's going to work, and then there'll be time for your questions at the end.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: First of all, why are we doing this? A lot of people assume it's mainly about cutting pollution, and of course fewer car trips will help with that. We'd also love to see visitors to the city using the bikes.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: But the real reason the council funded the scheme was a gap in the transport network. There's no direct bus between the railway station and the hospital and university campus, and that's a journey thousands of people make every day. The bikes are designed to fill that gap.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Now, the size of the fleet. Our original plan was to launch with 600 bikes. Unfortunately, our supplier has had delays at the factory, so on day one there'll be 450 bikes on the streets, spread across 40 docking stations. Of those, 300 are standard bikes and 150 are electric. The rest should arrive by the end of the summer.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: I get asked about the electric bikes more than anything else. Some people think they'll be restricted to adults over 18, but the minimum age is 16 for every bike in the fleet. And you can leave them at any docking station, just like the standard bikes.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: The one real difference is the cost. A standard bike is 20 cents a minute, and the electric ones are 35 cents a minute, because we have to pay for the charging.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: So, how do you actually use the scheme? The first step is to register. Most people will do it on the CityCycle app. If you don't have a smartphone, you can sign up at the kiosk at any docking station, using a bank card. We'd hoped to offer registration on our website too, but that won't be ready until later in the year.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Once you're registered, you can pay as you go, or you can save money with a pass. We thought about offering a weekly pass, but our research showed that very few people would use one, so we've gone for an annual pass and a monthly one. The annual pass works out cheapest if you ride every day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: To take a bike out, you open the app and scan the code on the bike. People tend to look for it on the seat or on the frame, but it's actually on the handlebars, right in the middle, so you can see it easily. The lock opens straight away.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Before you ride off, please check the brakes. Our maintenance team goes round every morning and checks the tyres and the lights, so you don't need to worry about those. But brakes can be damaged by one careless rider, so give them a quick squeeze before you set off.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: And if you do find a problem, please don't just leave the bike for the next person. Put it back in the dock and press the red button on the docking point. That locks the bike so no one else can take it, and it sends a message to our mechanics. You don't need to phone us or fill in a form.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Now, our launch month. We've planned a few things to get people on the bikes. Firstly, for the whole of the first month, any ride under 30 minutes will be completely free, so it's a great chance to try it out.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: We did look at giving away free helmets at the stations, but there are hygiene issues with sharing helmets, and it was too expensive to give everyone a new one, so you'll need to bring your own.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: What we will have is volunteers at the busiest stations in the first month, who'll show you how to use the app and how to adjust the seat height. Just look for the green jackets.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: A few people have asked whether students will get a discount. There's no student rate at the moment, though it's something we'll look at again next year. And I know everyone's waiting for the new cycle lane on Harbour Road. That won't be finished until next spring, I'm afraid, so please take care on that stretch.

lines.speaker: organiser
lines.text: Right, that's the overview. Let's open it up for questions. Yes, the lady at the front.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of the recording. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
